one_liner: Reference C header for the QOI lossless RGB/RGBA format: about 27x faster encode and 3.4x faster decode than libpng, with files about 17% larger.
what_it_does: qoi.h is a single-file, stb-style C library (define QOI_IMPLEMENTATION in one translation unit) that encodes and decodes the QOI image format, a frozen, unversioned lossless format for 8-bit RGB or RGBA pixels. The API is four functions: qoi_encode and qoi_decode work on memory buffers and return malloc'd results, while qoi_write and qoi_read wrap them with stdio (QOI_NO_STDIO drops those two). It is not PNG-compatible and not a libpng-style API: you get a whole image in, a whole buffer out, with no rows, streaming, metadata chunks or progressive callbacks.
how_it_is_fast: QOI has no entropy coder and no match search: each pixel is emitted as one of six byte-aligned chunks chosen by a fixed priority. These are a run of the previous pixel (up to 62), a 6-bit index into a 64-entry cache of recently seen colours hashed as (r*3 + g*5 + b*7 + a*11) & 63, a 1-byte delta of -2..1 per channel, a 2-byte 'luma' delta (green -32..31, red and blue relative to green -8..7), or a literal RGB or RGBA chunk. Encode and decode are one linear pass with a small branch tree per pixel and a 256-byte state table on the stack. libpng instead tries PNG row filters and then runs zlib deflate (LZ77 match search plus Huffman coding), and the match search is what costs it most of its encode time. The reference code is deliberately plain scalar C (no SIMD, one pixel per loop iteration even inside runs); the README says performance pull requests will probably not be accepted.
when_to_use: Writing lossless 8-bit RGB/RGBA frames where encode time dominates and you control the reader: screenshot capture, game or renderer frame dumps, intermediate pipeline images, asset caches. In the QOIR run it encoded 146.87 MPixels/s against libpng's 5.49 on one i5-10210U thread.

UI screenshots, icons and flat-colour art, where runs and the colour cache work best: screenshot_web 271.61 MPixels/s encode and 358.64 decode at CmpRatio 0.0835 (libpng 0.0757), icon_512 277.20 / 341.29.

Embedded, bootloader or freestanding code that needs a tiny auditable decoder: under 400 lines of C89-compatible implementation with only malloc/free/memset, endian-neutral byte I/O (the hash uses the r, g, b, a fields, not the packed word), and a frozen format with no version field.

When a non-PNG format is acceptable but tool support matters: the README lists QOI support in ImageMagick 7.1.0-20+, ffmpeg 5.1+, GIMP 3.0, KDE KImageFormats, Microsoft PowerToys, IrfanView and XnView MP, plus Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora and AUR packages.
when_not_to_use: When the output must be PNG: the catalogued fpnge encodes real PNG at 312.59 MPixels/s with CmpRatio 0.2798 in the same QOIR run, which is both faster than and slightly smaller than QOI overall (146.87, 0.2823), and fpng also decodes its own PNGs at 148.19. On photo subsets, though, fpnge files are larger than QOI's (photo_kodak 0.6218 vs 0.5829).

Photographs or anything where file size matters: QOI's ratio is about 17% worse than libpng's defaults overall and worse on photos (photo_wikipedia 0.6618 vs 0.5663, photo_tecnick 0.5992 vs 0.5011); Zpng gets 0.5190 on photo_wikipedia at similar speed, and WebP lossless reaches 0.1651 overall if encode time is not a concern.

Decoding untrusted files without your own limits: the header alone decides the allocation, so a 22-byte file can make qoi_decode allocate 80 MB (issue #340, open since June 2026), and up to 1.6 GB for a 400-megapixel RGBA header. Truncated or chunk-less streams decode 'successfully' instead of returning NULL. Check width*height against your own cap before calling it.

Grayscale, palette, 16-bit, HDR/float, premultiplied alpha, animation, ICC/EXIF metadata, or images over 400 million pixels: none of these is supported. The colorspace byte is informative only, and the reference loads the whole file into RAM (the README points to streaming implementations for huge images).

When you need the fastest QOI codec rather than the reference: the README says this implementation 'is not extensively optimized'. The catalogued qoixx (C++) and qoi-rust (Rust) produce the same format faster, and qoi-asm (x86-64 assembly, listed in the README in September 2026) claims 1.07x to 2.16x over qoi.h.

integration.dependencies: none beyond libc (malloc/free/memset; stdio for qoi_read/qoi_write unless QOI_NO_STDIO is defined). The qoibench tool also needs libpng, stb_image.h and stb_image_write.h, and qoiconv needs the two stb headers.
integration.min_toolchain: C89 (commits 'make qoi.h build using c89 compilers' and 'Remove single line comments to conform to c89 -pedantic', Dec 2021) or any C++ compiler; the Makefile builds qoiconv with -std=c99 -O3 and qoibench with -std=gnu99 -O3
integration.platforms: any; portable scalar C with no SIMD or intrinsics, and byte-wise big-endian header I/O, so endianness does not matter
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the functions keep all state (64-entry index, previous pixel) on the stack and have no mutable globals, so separate images can be coded on separate threads (inferred from the source).

gotchas: qoi_encode mallocs a worst-case buffer of width*height*(channels+1)+22 bytes and returns it without shrinking (about 10 MB for a 1080p RGBA frame, whatever the output size). There is no way to pass a preallocated buffer (issue #285, open); allocation can only be swapped globally at compile time with QOI_MALLOC/QOI_FREE, and results must be freed with the matching function.

qoi_decode never checks the 8-byte end marker or whether the chunks covered every pixel: when data runs out it fills the rest of the image with the last decoded colour and returns success (issue #340). Requesting channels=3 from an RGBA file silently drops alpha, and channels=4 from an RGB file yields alpha 255.
Sizes are int: qoi_decode takes int size and qoi_encode writes int *out_len, which is why the reference caps images at 400 million pixels (QOI_PIXELS_MAX) to stay under 2 GB.

Delta computation stores channel differences in signed char, which depends on implementation-defined narrowing (issues #254 and #328, both open). The qoi_rgba_t union is read through its packed .v member, which C allows but ISO C++ does not sanction. Both behave as intended on mainstream two's-complement compilers, but strict-UB checkers will flag them. There are no tags or releases (issue #261 'Tag a release?' open since 2023), so pin a commit hash.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick reference QOI when you want the most widely supported fast lossless format with a frozen spec and a vendorable header that reads like documentation. Use qoixx or qoi-rust for faster coding of the same files, fpnge or fpng when the output has to stay PNG, and QOIR or Zpng (custom formats too) when you want smaller files and faster decoding: QOIR_Lossless beat QOI on all three axes in the same run (0.2525, 168.90, 276.45).
verified_claims_summary: In Nigel Tao's QOIR harness (test/benchmarks.c, gettimeofday around repeated in-memory encode and decode calls with allocation included, single-threaded, gcc 10.2.1 with -O3 -march=native for the QOI adapter, Intel i5-10210U), on the qoiformat.org benchmark image suite, qoi.h encoded at 146.87 MPixels/s and decoded at 193.53 against Debian Bullseye's libpng simplified API at default compression (5.49 and 56.18), about 27x and 3.4x (derived from page data), with CmpRatio 0.2823 vs 0.2423. QOI's decode lead shrinks to about 1.4x against the Wuffs PNG decoder in the same run (140.79). The record's caveat that QOI compresses worse than libpng on every subset needs one correction: on textures_pk QOI is smaller (0.5645 vs 0.5991).
status_note: The format is final and qoi.h code last changed in April 2025 (the modulo-to-mask hash, merged May 2025; before that, stricter qoi_read/qoi_write error checks in June 2023). Commits since then, up to 2026-09-27, only add README links, so it is stable rather than actively developed. It is MIT-licensed, about 650 lines including the spec, and packaged by Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora, but has no tagged releases.
